body:
The historical setting of Jainism and Buddhism

During the middle of the 1st millennium BCE, northern India experienced important political, economic and social changes. Large territorial states known as Mahajanapadas developed, towns and trade expanded, and different religious teachers discussed the nature of human existence, suffering, moral conduct and liberation.

The Vedic tradition included sacrifices performed by priests and rules concerning social duties. Some thinkers questioned whether sacrifices, inherited social status or ritual knowledge alone could provide the highest spiritual goal. Jainism and Buddhism became influential within this wider atmosphere of religious discussion.

Both traditions are associated with the Shramana tradition, which emphasised renunciation, personal discipline and the possibility of liberation through individual effort. They did not accept the Vedas as the final authority for their religious teachings.

Jainism and Buddhism arose in a common intellectual environment, but their explanations of the soul, karma, discipline and liberation were not identical. Jainism accepted the existence of individual, enduring souls and placed exceptionally strong emphasis on non-violence and ascetic restraint. Buddhism rejected the idea of an eternal individual self and taught a Middle Way between self-indulgence and severe self-mortification.

The meaning of Jina and Tirthankara

A Jina is a spiritual victor who has overcome attachment and other passions. A Tirthankara, literally a ford-maker, is an enlightened teacher who shows others the path across the cycle of birth and rebirth towards liberation.

According to Jain tradition, there are 24 Tirthankaras in the present time cycle. They are regarded as teachers who reveal the path to liberation rather than as creator gods. The tradition therefore existed before Mahavira, who was its 24th Tirthankara.

The important Tirthankaras

  • 1st — Rishabhanatha: Also called Rishabhadeva or Adinatha, meaning the First Lord. He is the first Tirthankara in Jain tradition.
  • 22nd — Neminatha: An important Tirthankara in the Jain tradition.
  • 23rd — Parshvanatha: Also called Parshva. His teachings preceded those of Mahavira. Jain tradition associates him with 4 principal vows.
  • 24th — Vardhamana Mahavira: The last Tirthankara of the present time cycle, who gave renewed prominence to the Jain path of renunciation and the 5 great vows.

The numbers refer to positions in the traditional series of Tirthankaras, not to a historically established chronology for every teacher. The historical existence of Mahavira and Parshvanatha is generally accepted, while the earlier Tirthankaras are known primarily through Jain religious tradition.

Mahavira was not the 1st Tirthankara. He was the 24th. Calling him the founder of Jainism without qualification overlooks the earlier Tirthankara tradition.

Mahavira: Life and teachings

Vardhamana Mahavira lived during the period when the Mahajanapadas were developing. He was associated with the Kshatriya community and the Lichchhavis of the Vajji confederacy in the region of present-day Bihar. Jain traditions place his early life in the area associated with Vaishali.

According to the traditional account, he renounced household life at the age of 30. He practised severe ascetic discipline for approximately 12 years and then attained Kevala Jnana, or perfect knowledge. He subsequently taught a path based on non-violence, self-control, non-attachment and liberation from karmic bondage.

His message reached ordinary people through forms of Prakrit, the Middle Indo-Aryan languages used in everyday communication. The Jain canonical tradition is particularly associated with Ardhamagadhi Prakrit.

Mahavira's final liberation, or nirvana, is traditionally associated with Pavapuri in present-day Bihar. Jain Diwali commemorates this event.

Mahavira is commonly placed in the 6th century BCE in elementary historical accounts, although the exact dates of his life differ across Jain traditions and modern historical reconstructions. The dates 599–527 BCE belong to a widely cited traditional Shvetambara chronology and should not be treated as an undisputed historical dating.

Mahavira and the Buddha

Mahavira and Gautama Buddha were broadly contemporaries. Both belonged to the religious environment of the middle Ganga region, both renounced ordinary household life, and both taught that human beings could pursue liberation through their own conduct and understanding.

However, Mahavira's teaching placed stronger emphasis on rigorous asceticism, while the Buddha eventually rejected extreme bodily mortification. This contrast became one of the central differences between Jainism and Buddhism.

Prelims focus

  • Jain tradition recognises 24 Tirthankaras in the present time cycle.
  • Rishabhanatha, also called Adinatha, is the 1st Tirthankara.
  • Parshvanatha is the 23rd Tirthankara.
  • Vardhamana Mahavira is the 24th Tirthankara.
  • Mahavira renounced at about 30, practised asceticism for about 12 years and attained Kevala Jnana.
  • Mahavira's final liberation is associated with Pavapuri, Bihar.
  • Trap: Mahavira was the last Tirthankara of the present cycle, not the 1st.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6 History, Chapter 6, Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic, printed pp. 54–57, and Chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas, printed pp. 65–70; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part I, Class 12 History, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, printed pp. 84–90; Jainpedia, Jina, section The 24 Jinas, and Chronology, consulted 18 November 2026.]

body:
Why ethical discipline is central to Jainism

Jainism teaches that living beings possess souls and that actions have consequences for those souls. Actions influenced by attachment, anger, greed and other passions contribute to karmic bondage. Liberation requires controlling conduct, reducing attachment and eventually eliminating the karma associated with the soul.

For this reason, Jain ethics is not simply a collection of rules governing social behaviour. It is an essential part of the spiritual path towards moksha, or release from the cycle of birth and rebirth.

Ahimsa: The central Jain principle

Ahimsa means non-violence or non-injury towards living beings. In Jainism, it requires exceptional care to avoid harm through bodily actions, speech and intentions.

Jainism extends moral concern beyond human beings and large animals to insects, plants and other forms of life. Jain doctrine also recognises forms of life associated with earth and water. This explains why traditional Jain ascetics try to minimise even unintended injury.

For example, care in walking, handling water and obtaining food reflects the belief that seemingly ordinary activities can harm small living beings. Strict vegetarian practices are also closely associated with the Jain commitment to ahimsa.

Ahimsa is the most prominent Jain vow, but it does not stand alone. Truthfulness, honesty, sexual restraint and non-possession are also necessary because falsehood, theft and excessive attachment arise from passions that obstruct liberation.

The 5 great vows of Jainism

Mahavira's ethical discipline is expressed through the 5 Mahavratas, or great vows. They are observed in their strict form by Jain monks and nuns.

  • Ahimsa — Non-violence: Avoid injuring living beings. This includes careful control of actions and intentions.
  • Satya — Truthfulness: Refrain from lying and from speech that causes injury. Truthfulness must be practised consistently with non-violence.
  • Asteya or Achaurya — Non-stealing: Do not take what has not been willingly given.
  • Brahmacharya — Celibacy: Observe complete sexual restraint in the ascetic life.
  • Aparigraha — Non-possession or non-attachment: Renounce attachment to possessions and worldly acquisitions.

These vows are related. For instance, attachment to wealth can encourage stealing or dishonesty. Aparigraha addresses the attachment itself, while asteya and satya govern the conduct that might result from it.

Parshvanatha's 4 vows and Mahavira's 5 vows

According to the traditional Jain account, the 23rd Tirthankara, Parshvanatha, taught 4 principal restraints: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing and non-possession.

Mahavira presented celibacy as a separate 5th vow. In explanations of the earlier 4-vow discipline, sexual restraint was understood within the wider requirement of non-possession or non-attachment.

Parshvanatha: 4 vows. Mahavira: 5 vows. The separately stated vow associated with Mahavira is Brahmacharya, or celibacy.

Mahavrata and Anuvrata: Different levels of observance

Jainism distinguishes between the discipline of renunciants and that of ordinary householders.

Mahavratas for monks and nuns

The Mahavratas are the great vows followed in their strict form by monks and nuns. Monastic life involves renunciation, restraint and disciplined efforts to avoid harm and attachment.

Anuvratas for householders

The Anuvratas are limited or lesser forms of the principal vows. They allow lay followers to observe Jain ethical principles while fulfilling family and occupational responsibilities.

For example, the celibacy required of a renunciant is different from the sexual restraint expected of a lay householder, whose vow restricts sexual relations to their spouse. Similarly, the renunciation of possessions expected in the monastic life is more extensive than the restraint practised by householders, whose vow requires setting limits on their possessions.

The distinction matters because Jainism recognises a religious community consisting of both ascetics and lay supporters. Classical Jain teaching presents complete renunciation as the path to final liberation, while lay conduct supports spiritual progress and the monastic community.

Comparison with Buddhist ethical discipline

Buddhism also prohibits harmful actions and values truthful speech, non-stealing, restraint and compassion. However, it does not prescribe the same degree of ascetic severity as the Jain monastic ideal.

Early Buddhist teaching places disciplined ethical conduct within the Noble Eightfold Path and rejects extreme self-mortification. The distinction is therefore not that Jainism teaches morality while Buddhism does not. Both teach morality, but they differ in the severity and philosophical role of ascetic practices.

Prelims focus

  • Ahimsa is the central ethical principle of Jainism.
  • The 5 Mahavratas are Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Brahmacharya and Aparigraha.
  • Parshvanatha is traditionally associated with 4 vows.
  • Mahavira separately emphasised Brahmacharya as the 5th vow.
  • Mahavratas are the strict vows of ascetics; Anuvratas are limited vows for lay followers.
  • Trap: Aparigraha means non-possession or non-attachment; Asteya means non-stealing.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6 History, Chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas, printed pp. 69–70; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part I, Class 12 History, Theme 4, section 3, Beyond Worldly Pleasures, printed p. 88; Jainpedia, Five Fundamental Vows, sections Fundamental Vows and Two Versions, and Vows, sections Mendicant Vows and Lay Vows, consulted 18 November 2026; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Jaina Philosophy, section 1, Ethics of Renunciation, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The same 5 Jain vows lead to strict Mahavrata observance by monks and nuns and limited Anuvrata observance by householders.
pictures.caption: The same 5 ethical principles are observed with different degrees of restraint.

title: Ahimsa and the Five Great Vows: The Ethical Discipline of Jainism

body:
The fundamental problem: Bondage of the soul

Jainism teaches that the universe contains both living and non-living realities. The central distinction is between Jiva, the living soul, and Ajiva, non-living reality.

Jiva is a conscious, enduring individual soul. Ajiva includes matter and other non-living principles. Jainism does not teach that all living beings share one identical individual soul; each living being possesses its own soul.

According to Jain philosophy, the soul is naturally capable of perfect knowledge and freedom. However, it becomes associated with karma through its activities and passions. This association prevents the soul from manifesting its pure nature.

Jain understanding of karma

In Jainism, karma is understood as subtle material matter that becomes associated with the soul. Actions driven by attachment and passions contribute to this bondage and influence future experiences and rebirths.

A soul bound by karma remains within samsara, the cycle of birth, death and rebirth. Freedom requires both preventing further karmic bondage and removing previously accumulated karma through disciplined conduct, restraint and austerities.

This is different from the Buddhist account, which also accepts karma and rebirth but does not explain them through an eternal individual soul bound by karmic matter.

The Jain Triratna: 3 jewels of liberation

The Triratna, or 3 jewels of Jainism, are Samyak Darshana, Samyak Jnana and Samyak Charitra. They mean Right Faith, Right Knowledge and Right Conduct.

Samyak Darshana: Right Faith or Right View

Right Faith means a correct understanding of and confidence in the fundamental truths taught by the Jinas. It includes accepting the reality of the soul, karma, moral responsibility and the possibility of liberation.

It is not merely unquestioning belief. It refers to a proper orientation towards reality and the path to freedom.

Samyak Jnana: Right Knowledge

Right Knowledge means correctly understanding reality. A person should understand the difference between soul and non-soul, the causes of karmic bondage and the principles required for liberation.

Knowledge without appropriate understanding can lead to mistaken action. Jainism therefore links correct knowledge to right faith and conduct.

Samyak Charitra: Right Conduct

Right Conduct means putting correct faith and knowledge into practice through non-violence, truthfulness, restraint, detachment and disciplined living.

It is not sufficient to understand non-violence intellectually while continuing to injure living beings deliberately. Knowledge must guide actual conduct.

How the 3 jewels work together

The 3 jewels are complementary requirements of the path rather than independent alternatives.

  • Right Faith establishes the correct spiritual orientation.
  • Right Knowledge provides an accurate understanding of the soul, karma and liberation.
  • Right Conduct applies that understanding to life and helps overcome karmic bondage.

For example, a person may accept ahimsa as a true moral principle and understand that unnecessary injury creates karmic consequences. The next requirement is to practise non-violence consistently. The combination of belief, understanding and conduct explains the practical meaning of the Jain Triratna.

Kevala Jnana and Moksha

Kevala Jnana means complete or omniscient knowledge. A person who attains it is a Kevalin. Jain tradition holds that Mahavira attained Kevala Jnana after prolonged ascetic discipline.

Moksha is the final liberation of the soul from karmic bondage and the cycle of rebirth. Jainism teaches that the liberated soul exists in its pure state, free from further rebirth.

Kevala Jnana and final liberation are closely related but should not be treated as identical events in Mahavira's life. According to Jain tradition, he attained omniscience while living and reached final liberation at the end of his earthly life.

Why the idea of an eternal soul matters

The Jain belief in an enduring individual soul is a major philosophical difference from Buddhism.

Jainism explains rebirth as the continuing journey of a soul affected by karma. Buddhism explains continuity through conditioned processes without accepting an unchanging individual soul that passes from one body to another.

Prelims focus

  • Jiva means the living, conscious soul; Ajiva means non-living reality.
  • Jainism accepts enduring individual souls.
  • Jain karma is understood as subtle matter associated with the soul.
  • Jain Triratna: Right Faith, Right Knowledge and Right Conduct.
  • Kevala Jnana means perfect or omniscient knowledge.
  • Moksha means final liberation from karma and rebirth.
  • Trap: Jain Triratna is not the same as the Buddhist 3 jewels of Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha.

[References: NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part I, Class 12 History, Theme 4, Beyond Worldly Pleasures, printed pp. 88–89; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Jaina Philosophy, sections 1.3, The Categories of Reality, 1.4, Liberation as Unobstructed Knowledge, and 2.4, Of Self and Karma, consulted 18 November 2026; Jainpedia, Vows, opening discussion of faith, knowledge and conduct, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Karma binds the individual soul to rebirth; all 3 Jain jewels guide the removal of bondage toward moksha, distinct from omniscient knowledge.
pictures.caption: The Jain path connects right understanding and disciplined conduct with freedom from karmic bondage.

title: Jain Triratna, Jiva, Karma and the Path to Moksha
